content.overview: Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides for a perpetual injunction. Subject to the other provisions of the Chapter, it may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour, whether express or implied. Where the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to or enjoyment of property, the court may grant it where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff, where there is no standard for ascertaining the actual damage, where money compensation would not be adequate relief, or where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of proceedings. A perpetual injunction is final relief. It is not a temporary injunction and not specific performance.
content.study: Identify the obligation in the plaintiff's favour. For a property invasion, use one of the four section 38(3) grounds. Do not grant it for a contract section 14 will not enforce.

learningObjectives: Separate a perpetual injunction from specific performance.
enhancement.definition: A perpetual injunction under section 38 prevents breach of an obligation owed to the plaintiff, including a property invasion in the cases the section lists.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The injunction prevents a breach. It does not itself perform a contract that section 14 bars, and it is granted subject to the rest of the Chapter.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, section 38. Section 41 lists injunctions that are refused and is not opened as a new topic.
essentialIngredients: Obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour
For property, trustee, no damage standard, inadequate money relief, or multiplicity
Subject to the other provisions of the Chapter
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Subsection (1) makes the injunction subject to the other provisions of the Chapter. Subsection (2) says it may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour, expressly or by implication. Subsection (3) is the property case. The defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property, and one of four conditions is met: the defendant is a trustee of the property for the plaintiff; no standard exists for ascertaining the actual damage caused or likely to be caused; the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; or the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings. Adequacy of compensation is a section 38(3) ground. It is not the section 10 test for specific performance. A temporary injunction is a Code of Civil Procedure remedy and is not this section.
examples: A defendant threatens to cut timber on the plaintiff's land, and money cannot measure the loss. Section 38(3) can be considered.
A trustee deals with trust property against the beneficiary. The trustee ground is in section 38(3).
A plaintiff seeks a perpetual injunction to compel personal service. Section 14 and the Chapter's refusal provisions have to be checked before section 38 is used.
enhancement.problemApplication: Name the obligation, the threatened breach, and, if property is involved, the subsection (3) ground. Keep the order preventive and final.

keyTakeaways: The injunction prevents breach of an obligation.
It may be express or implied.
Property cases use the four subsection (3) grounds.
Inadequate money relief is a property ground, not the section 10 test.
It is final relief, not a temporary injunction.
